\section{Introduction}
Radio phone-ins, meetings and street interviews in India mix several speakers, overlapping
speech, noise and languages within one sentence. Our system outputs a speaker timeline,
a speaker-separated transcript, a translation, a summary and tags, using only pretrained models. We contribute (i)~a modular pipeline whose stages
are swappable through config and pass failures through rather than halting, and (ii)~a
reproducible benchmark of the alternatives at every stage.

\section{Background and related work}
Diarization embeds short windows and clusters them. We use ECAPA-TDNN embeddings~\cite{ecapa}
with spectral clustering~\cite{ng2001spectral} and compare them with GMMs and the end-to-end
pyannote pipeline~\cite{pyannote}. SepFormer~\cite{sepformer} separates overlapped speakers. For
ASR we compare Whisper~\cite{whisper} (via faster-whisper), MMS-1B-all~\cite{mms}, IndicWav2Vec
and Sarvam's commercial model. Whisper's published Indic numbers are optimistic because its
normaliser deletes vowel signs; correctly scored, Whisper-medium exceeds 100\% WER on most Indic
FLEURS languages~\cite{thennal}.

\section{Method}
(1)~Peak normalisation and silence trimming. (2)~Diarization: energy VAD, 1.5\,s windows, ECAPA
embeddings, cosine affinity, spectral clustering with $K$ set by the largest eigengap.
(3)~Separation only on overlapped regions; streams are assigned to speakers by embedding
similarity, so single-speaker audio is never distorted. (4)~ASR per speaker turn. (5)~Gemini~3.5
Flash-Lite (free API, temperature 0.2, JSON output) returns cleaned text, language labels,
translations, a 2--4 sentence summary and tags. The prompt forbids facts absent from the
transcript; a local Ollama model is a config toggle for offline use. WER and CER are pooled over
clips, and both sides pass through one Indic-safe normaliser (NFC, indic-nlp canonicalisation,
punctuation removed, vowel signs never stripped). Runs log seeds, model versions and git SHA.

\section{Experimental setup}
833 clips from IndicVoices (260), Nirantar (260) and Vaani (198; noisy, phone-recorded), plus 40
English and 24 Hindi--English code-switch clips. We score 782, excluding Sindhi, whose
references are Devanagari while systems write Perso-Arabic. Diarization uses 10 sequential
multi-speaker clips, 24 synthetic two-speaker mixtures and the code-switch clips; separation uses
the mixtures. AIR-RS-DB needs a paid IEEE DataPort subscription and was not used. Metrics:
WER/CER, DER (no collar, overlap scored), SI-SNRi, and LLM rewrite CER and grounding.
Hardware: one RTX~3050 (4\,GB). Sarvam and the baseline faster-whisper run were produced
separately and re-scored with our scorer.

\textbf{ASR.} Sarvam wins all 14 languages, from 5.4\% WER (English) to 50.6\% (Tamil). Among
free systems MMS wins except on Hindi, where IndicWav2Vec is better (36.9\% vs 40.7\%), and on
English, where faster-whisper is. Noisy Vaani is hardest (39.1\% vs 17.3\% on Nirantar for Sarvam). In Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam, CER is a third to a quarter of WER: one word
packs several morphemes, so one wrong suffix costs the whole word.
\textbf{Diarization.} Spectral beats GMM in every setting, because a full-covariance GMM overfits
a few dozen windows per clip. ECAPA picks the right speaker count on 60\% of sequential clips,
MFCC on 20\%. Both pyannote systems output one speaker on 22--23 of 24 code-switch clips,
although the halves are different voices (median ECAPA cosine 0.058).
\textbf{Separation.} SepFormer-Libri2Mix gives 15.8\,dB SI-SNRi on overlaps and assigns 75\% of
streams correctly, against 6.6\,dB and 58\% for WSJ0-2mix. Separating everything instead of
only overlaps raises WER (Table~\ref{tab:asr}).
\textbf{Preprocessing.} Level and filter changes stay within 0.25\,pp of raw audio; denoising
adds 8.7\,pp WER (9.1\,pp on noisy Vaani), so we do not denoise.
\textbf{LLM} (34 transcripts). Gemini changed 2.2\% of characters, labelled 97\% of segments
correctly, invented 0 numbers and took 11\,s. Local Qwen2.5-Coder 7B changed 11.4\%
and took 27\,s.

\section{Discussion and limitations}\label{sec:disc}
\textbf{faster-whisper.} Whisper's byte-level tokenizer spends about two tokens per character in
Bengali, Gujarati, Malayalam or Punjabi (0.4 in English), but faster-whisper allows 224 new tokens
per 30\,s window. 90 of 782 baseline outputs end in a half-written character, and capped clips
cause about half of all word errors, either truncated or filled by a repetition loop that
temperature~0 never retries. $\le$15\,s VAD chunks, a 400-token budget and compression-gated
temperature fallback fix this (84.5\%\,$\to$\,75.5\%). What remains is the model:
\texttt{large-v3} writes 13 of 84 clips in the wrong script with the language forced, and has 69.4\% WER on right-script clips, in line with published
zero-shot results~\cite{thennal,vividh}.
\textbf{Limitations.} The code-switch reference labels whole stitched clips as speech, so 46\% of
its speaker time is silence; every system scores 49--64\% DER against it, so we report
VAD-tightened turns. Next we would try IndicConformer and
Indic-fine-tuned Whisper~\cite{vistaar}.

\section{Conclusion}
Chained in the right order, pretrained models give a usable pipeline: ECAPA + spectral
diarization, overlap-only SepFormer, an Indic-trained ASR and Gemini cleanup. Most remaining
error is ASR on low-resource languages.
